claims.text: Catalytic performance of transition-metal catalysts is controlled by the position of the d-band center.
Alloying can shift the d-band center relative to the Fermi level.
A shift in the d-band center alters the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates.
Changes in intermediate adsorption energies govern catalytic activity and selectivity.
Introducing Ti or Pd into Pt nanoparticles can form bimetallic alloy nanoparticles.
Varying the amount or identity of the second metal can deliberately tune the d-band center relative to pure Pt.
The alloying-induced d-band-center change modifies the surface electronic structure.
The modified surface electronic structure changes the adsorption energies of key intermediates.
A d-band-center shift changes the density of electronic states near the Fermi level.
The density of states near the Fermi level controls the binding strength of reactants and intermediates.
An optimal d-band-center shift balances adsorption strong enough for activation with binding weak enough for facile desorption.
Balancing activation and desorption enhances catalytic turnover.
Pt-based bimetallic catalysts with a moderate d-band-center shift will have greater catalytic activity than pure Pt under matched conditions.
Pt-based bimetallic catalysts with a moderate d-band-center shift will have improved selectivity relative to pure Pt.
Excessive or insufficient d-band-center shifts will produce lower catalytic performance than a moderate shift.
The proposed relationship applies to transition-metal-catalyzed reactions in which adsorption energies are critical, including CO oxidation and hydrogen evolution.

The proposed relationship is expected to hold only when particle size, morphology, support properties, and reaction conditions are controlled and no significant morphological or compositional changes occur during operation.
If catalysts with significantly different d-band centers show similar or non-optimized activity or selectivity relative to pure Pt, the proposed governing relationship is rejected.
